title: React Conditional Rendering with the Ternary Operator & AND Operator
summary: Builds a login screen that shows either a greeting or a login form depending on an isLoggedIn flag. Starts with an if/else helper function, refactors the form into reusable Login and Input components, then replaces the function with an inline ternary and finally the && short-circuit pattern.

concepts.heading: The goal: show different components for different state
points: Typical use: a logged-out visitor sees a login form, a logged-in user sees a greeting or dashboard. The same App decides which one to render from a single boolean.

Start from the provided CodeSandbox (fork it). It has one App component with a heading and a hard-coded form. A module-level variable isLoggedIn (false at first) stands in for the result of authentication.
Rule of thumb: check one value, render one of several components.

concepts.heading: First approach: a helper function with if/else
points: Write a function (e.g. renderConditionally) that tests isLoggedIn. If true it returns the h1 greeting element, otherwise it returns the form markup.
Call it inside the JSX with curly braces and parentheses: {renderConditionally()}. The braces switch from JSX to JavaScript, and the parentheses actually invoke the function.

Comparing with === true is redundant because isLoggedIn is already a boolean; writing if (isLoggedIn) is enough. Flip the variable between true and false and the page updates to show the other branch.
It works but is verbose for something done constantly in React, which motivates the shorter forms below.

concepts.heading: Single responsibility: extract Login and Input components
points: Each component should do one job (single responsibility principle). The inline form markup is moved out of App.
Challenge in the lecture: create a Login component holding the whole form, and an Input component for each field, configured with props so it can be reused.
Login.jsx: import React, define function Login returning the form, export default Login. In App, import Login from './Login' and render <Login />.

Input.jsx: returns a single <input>. Because the two inputs differ in type and placeholder, those become props: <Input type="text" placeholder="Username" /> and <Input type="password" placeholder="Password" />.
Inside Input, read props.type and props.placeholder in curly braces: <input type={props.type} placeholder={props.placeholder} />.
The page looks identical afterwards, but responsibilities are split: Input = one field, Login = whole form, App = which one is shown.

concepts.heading: Why an if statement cannot go inside JSX braces
points: Curly braces in JSX accept only expressions (anything that resolves to a single value). An if/else, a loop or a switch is a statement and causes a syntax error if pasted in.
So the conditional logic needs to be rewritten as an expression to live inline where the output is rendered.

concepts.heading: Ternary operator
points: Syntax: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. The ? and : separate three expressions; because all three are expressions, the whole thing is one expression and legal inside JSX.

Applied here: {isLoggedIn ?

Hello

: }. Read it as 'is isLoggedIn true? then the h1, else the Login component'.
The condition can be the boolean itself; no need for == true.
Toggling the variable swaps which component appears, with no helper function needed.

concepts.heading: Rendering nothing: null in the false branch
points: Sometimes you only want something when a condition holds. Demo: const currentTime = new Date().getHours(), which returns the hour 0-23.

{currentTime > 12 ?

: null} shows the heading after noon and nothing before. React renders nothing for null.
Testing trick: temporarily construct a Date for a fixed time (e.g. new Date(2019, 11, 1, 9)) to try morning and evening cases.

concepts.heading: The && (AND) short-circuit pattern
points: In JavaScript, a && b only evaluates b when a is truthy. If a is falsy, evaluation stops and the result is a. This is called short-circuit evaluation.

In JSX: {currentTime > 12 &&

Why are you still working?

}. When the left side is true the right side (the element) is evaluated and rendered; when false it is skipped and React renders nothing for false.
It is equivalent to the ternary with null in the else branch, just shorter. Using it is optional; you will see it very often in real-world React code.
When reading such code, the intent is not to test that both sides are true, but to render the right side only if the left side is true.
(Extra) currentTime > 12 is false during the 12:00-12:59 hour (getHours() returns 12), so the message actually appears from 13:00; use >= 12 if noon itself should count.

(Extra) The element on the right of && or inside a ternary branch can span several lines; wrap it in parentheses, e.g. {cond && (
...
)}, so the JSX parses cleanly.

concepts.heading: Extra notes
points: (Extra) Beware of numbers on the left: {count && <p/>} renders a literal 0 when count is 0, because 0 is a valid renderable value. Use count > 0 && ... instead.
(Extra) true, false, null and undefined are all ignored by React when rendering, which is why both null and a false && result show nothing.

pitfalls: Pasting an if/else into JSX braces gives a syntax error because it is a statement.
Forgetting the parentheses when calling the helper function: {renderConditionally} passes the function itself instead of its result.
Confusing && in JSX with a 'both must be true' check; it is a render-if guard.

The reference repo names the form component LoginForm and adds a small Button component (type and text props), differing from the lecture's Login/Input split; it also writes isLoggedIn == true in the ternary (redundant) and leaves the old helper function commented out (with a misspelt name). The notes' solution uses the lecture naming.
